name: PT MNC Tourism Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: MNC Tourism Indonesia: an asset-rich estate priced as a financing vehicle
frontmatter.summary: KPIG owns Jakarta office towers, Park Hyatt Jakarta and the Bali and Lido resort estates, carried at a deep discount to book. Operating returns are thin and the shares have de-rated with the rest of the MNC group. We rate BUY on the balance sheet, not on the earnings.
thesis: The market capitalisation is a fraction of pre-revaluation book equity, so the shares are a claim on land and hotels rather than on earnings; on our numbers the operating business alone does not carry the debt at the cost of capital.
FY2025 profit was flattered by a one-off apartment and other properties sale; underlying EBITDA is roughly a third of the reported figure, and that is what we capitalise in the DCF.

The target is the asset value, because listed Indonesian hotel and property owners trade at a peer median multiple of book, several times the multiple the market applies to KPIG's equity - and the multiple is applied to book net of the revaluation surplus, not to reported equity.
Hospitality is the only segment with pricing power, and occupancy recovery plus the Park Hyatt and Lido ramp drives the next three years.
Governance is what the discount is for — related-party revenue, related-party receivables, serial rights issues and no dividend. A discounted issue is the main per-share risk.
The asset discount closes only on a sale, an injection or a change of control, none of which we put in the base case.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and annual report
Lido estate phase opening and hospitality guidance

blocks.text: We initiate on PT MNC Tourism Indonesia (KPIG, formerly PT MNC Land) with a **BUY** rating and a target of **Rp51**, a total return of **74.4%** from the last close of Rp29. The company is not an earnings story. It is a Jakarta and Bali property estate with a hotel business attached, and the market values it as though the estate belonged to the lenders.

The variant view is about what the market is actually pricing. The equity is capitalised at 3,112,072,423,481 rupiah against reported equity of IDR29,950.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S2], of which IDR10,239.4bn is a land revaluation surplus booked through other comprehensive income [S3]. Strip the surplus and equity is still a large multiple of the market capitalisation. On our numbers the operating business, capitalised at our cost of capital, is worth less than net debt: the DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR826.6bn against net debt above that figure [S3]. A buyer at today's price is paying for the balance sheet, not the cash flows, and paying very little for it. That is the whole argument, and it is also the argument's weakness: a balance sheet only pays out if someone sells it, and the controlling family has shown no appetite to.

Three things move the value. First, hospitality: the hotel, resort and golf segment produced IDR1,059.8bn of revenue and IDR450.0bn of gross profit in FY2025 [S3], and it is the only segment with genuine pricing power. Second, the property cycle in Jakarta and Bali: office rental is a related-party rent roll that shrank in FY2025, property management is a genuine service business but earns a margin near four per cent, and the apartment line's FY2025 result is not repeatable [S3]. Third, the capital structure: another discounted equity issue, which the group has used before, would transfer value from minorities to the parent faster than operations can create it.

We are deliberately not capitalising the FY2025 headline. Reported net profit attributable to the parent was IDR717.2bn [S3], but IDR568.8bn of gross profit came from the apartment and other properties segment, which did twelve times the prior year's revenue at a nine-tenths gross margin [S3]. Nine-month 2026 revenue of IDR1,660.0bn [S2] is the cleaner guide and implies a full year well below FY2025. Our forecasts are built on that cleaner base; the target itself is asset-based, because the operating business does not carry the debt.

Indonesian tourism and hospitality has recovered unevenly since the pandemic, with international
arrivals concentrated in Bali and a domestic market that carries most hotel demand. Property
companies of this type are typically valued on a discount to net asset value rather than on
earnings, because development cycles are long and reported profit is dominated by revaluation and
disposal gains. Family-controlled conglomerates in Indonesia frequently trade at persistent
discounts to book for governance reasons that are structural rather than cyclical.

KPIG is the tourism and property arm of the MNC group. It was renamed from PT MNC Land to PT MNC Tourism Indonesia in July 2025 to reflect a strategic pivot toward hospitality, and it reports four segments: hotel, resort and golf; apartment and other properties; property management and other services; and office space rental [S3]. The company is domiciled in Jakarta, employs about 241.0 people, and all of its operations are in Indonesia [S3].

The revenue mix in FY2025 was dominated by two blocks. Hotel, resort and golf turned over IDR1,059.8bn with IDR450.0bn of gross profit, a margin consistent with a premium hotel portfolio operating at city and resort rates [S3]. Property management and other services is the largest service line at IDR829.8bn of revenue but earned only IDR33.3bn of gross profit, a margin near four per cent, and it was of a similar size in FY2024 [S3]. Office space rental is small — IDR103.8bn of revenue — but earned IDR59.6bn of gross profit, a margin in the high fifties, which tells you the rents are set between related parties rather than in an open market: the segment exists to house group companies. Apartment and other properties swung from IDR53.0bn of revenue in FY2024 to IDR621.8bn in FY2025 on a single transaction at a nine-tenths gross margin [S3]; that is the one-off, and it sits in the apartment line, not in property management.

The operating assets are the reason to look at the company at all. The portfolio includes Park Hyatt Jakarta, which the company reports won a MICHELIN Key award in the third quarter of 2026 [S2], resort and golf assets in Bali, and the Lido estate in Bogor, a large integrated tourism development that has absorbed capital for years. The balance sheet carries property, plant and equipment of IDR22,429.4bn [S0], the bulk of it land and buildings at revalued amounts. The company also leases office space to affiliated MNC entities and provides property management services to them, which is why related-party revenue was IDR424.7bn in FY2025 [S3] — a material share of the consolidated top line.

Strategy, as the company describes it, is to reposition the portfolio around premium hospitality and experience-led tourism: hotel refurbishments, food and beverage concepts, and the phased opening of the Lido estate [S3]. There is no disclosed target for room count, revenue or returns, and no capital-allocation framework that we could find in the annual report — a gap that matters because the company has been a net consumer of capital for at least four years [S0].

The group structure is the single most important fact about the equity. KPIG sits under the MNC group controlled by the Tanoesoedibjo family, with PT MNC Asia Holding as the parent entity [S3]. The exchange's free-float registry records a free float of 68.0% [S0], which is the figure we use; the data pack's insider percentage of 76.3% is not reconcilable with it, and we flag the conflict rather than publish both as fact. On the registry figure the fifteen per cent minimum-float deadline is not a live index risk. That combination — a controlling family, a listed float, and a web of related-party contracts — defines the governance discount the shares carry. KPIG is a challenger in Indonesian hospitality by room count and a marginal player in Jakarta office rental; its position is built on land acquired decades ago and on group demand, not on brand or distribution advantages a competitor could not replicate.

The industry backdrop in 2025 was soft. Occupancy at star-rated hotels across Indonesia fell to 49.3%, a decline of more than three points on the prior year, with the steepest drop in the four-star category [S3]. The company nevertheless projects a positive 2026 on the back of national tourism recovery and government arrival targets [S3]. Our base case takes the middle path: modest occupancy recovery in Bali and Jakarta luxury, flat to slightly lower rates in the mass-market four-star segment where KPIG does not compete directly.

Commercial property is the second driver. The company cites a commercial property supply index up by a low-single-digit percentage year on year in the fourth quarter of 2025 and a demand index up by less than one percent [S3]. That is a market with more supply than demand: office rent rolls shrank in FY2025 and property management, the labour-intensive service line, earns a gross margin near four per cent [S3]. We forecast no rent growth in real terms. Apartment demand is similarly tepid. For a company whose land bank is the asset, a flat property market means the discount to book does not close on its own.

Regulation cuts both ways. The most important rule change for the share price is not a tourism rule at all: the exchange lowered the minimum share price to Rp1, removing the floor that had supported the group's smaller-capitalisation shares and triggering a wave of limit-down sessions across MNC-group stocks in late September 2026 [S5]. KPIG lost more than half its value in the weeks after the change and traded at Rp29 a month later [S4], [S0]. That is a market-structure event, not an operating one, and it is the largest single explanation for the twelve-month decline from Rp286 to Rp24 [S0].

On competitive positioning, the moat is location, not brand. Park Hyatt Jakarta and the Bali resort assets sit on land that cannot be reproduced at today's prices, and that is a genuine barrier to entry. Against that, the company has no distribution advantage, no loyalty economics of its own (the hotels are managed under third-party brands), and no evidence of pricing power above the market: hotel gross margin in FY2025 was high but flattered by mix, and the segment's operating margin after allocated costs was far lower [S3]. Five forces, in short: low threat of new supply in luxury Jakarta, high threat in mid-market Bali, weak supplier power, customers with real choice, and — decisively — a landlord whose counterparties are often its own affiliates.

External influences we watch are the rupiah, domestic interest rates and the government's tourism arrival targets [S3]. The macro desk is cautious on rate-sensitive Indonesian domestic cyclicals this cycle, a headwind for the property leg and a reason to keep hospitality as the growth engine in our numbers. The competitive set is fragmented: listed peers own individual resorts and are valued as development options, while KPIG's edge is the size of its Jakarta and Bali land position.

The starting point is a restatement. The data pack shows FY2025 D&A of a few billion rupiah against property, plant and equipment of IDR22,429.4bn [S0]. That is not credible for a hotel and office landlord, and it is not what the accounts say: depreciation charged in FY2025 was IDR143.5bn and in FY2024 IDR141.1bn [S3]. The pack captured only the depreciation line inside cost of revenues; the remainder sits in general and administrative expenses [S3]. The company's own financial highlights confirm the corrected figure — it reports EBITDA of IDR829.0bn against operating income of IDR685.6bn, a difference that reconciles to our restated depreciation [S3]. Everything below uses that basis, and the engine rebuilds history from it.

Revenue in FY2025 was IDR2,615.3bn, up sharply on IDR1,770.1bn in FY2024 [S3]. The increase is almost entirely one line. Apartment and other properties reported IDR621.8bn of revenue and IDR568.8bn of gross profit in FY2025, against IDR53.0bn of revenue the year before [S3]. A segment that multiplies revenue twelvefold and earns a gross margin above ninety percent has sold something, not built a recurring business. We therefore treat that gross profit as non-recurring. On a consistent recurring base — total revenue less the apartment segment, total gross profit less the apartment segment — FY2025 gross margin was 27.2%, and selling plus general and administrative expenses were 21.4% of recurring revenue [S3]. Those are the levels we carry into FY2026E. The prior draft's smaller opex ratio came from adding back the prior-year apartment revenue without its cost; the numbers here use the same denominator on both sides.

That is the bridge to our forecast. Nine-month 2026 revenue was IDR1,660.0bn with hospitality contributing IDR898.8bn [S2]. Annualising the nine months, and allowing for a seasonally weak fourth quarter that has been loss-making at the operating line in each of the last two years [S0], we forecast FY2026E revenue of IDR2,209.9bn, a decline on FY2025 that is entirely the absence of the one-off. From FY2027E we grow the top line at a mid-single-digit rate driven by hospitality occupancy and rate, with property flat.

Margins follow. We forecast a gross margin of 27.2% rising to 28.5% by FY2030E as hotel revenue becomes a larger share of the mix, and SG&A at 21.4% of revenue — the FY2025 recurring level [S3]. That gives EBIT of IDR128.2bn and EBITDA of IDR271.8bn. This is the number that matters: reported EBITDA of IDR829.0bn in FY2025 is roughly two and a half times the underlying run rate, and anyone valuing KPIG off the headline is overpaying by that factor.

Profit does not follow EBITDA down, and the bridge needs stating because the nine-month result is higher than our full year. Nine-month 2026 net profit was IDR361.1bn [S2] against a full-year forecast here of IDR381.7bn. The difference is not a fourth-quarter collapse; it is the non-operating line. Operating profit of IDR128.2bn cannot produce a nine-month profit of that size on its own, and the cash-flow statement names the source: disposals of financial assets and investments [S3]. We therefore carry the FY2026E non-operating allowance at IDR400.0bn, the run-rate the nine months imply, and fade it to nothing by FY2031E as the portfolio is consumed. On that basis the full year lands a little above the nine months rather than below it, which is the test the earlier draft failed.

Cash flow is where the story gets uncomfortable. Free cash flow was IDR-223.8bn in FY2025 only because capex fell to IDR616.6bn from IDR1,862.7bn the year before [S0]. Over three years the company has spent more on property, plant and equipment than it generated from operations, funded by a rights issue and by related-party borrowings. Our forecast keeps capex at IDR442.0bn in FY2026E, fading as the Lido phases complete, and even then free cash flow barely turns positive. That is the central financial fact: this is a business that consumes its own cash generation to maintain an estate that earns a low return.

The balance sheet is levered but cheaply so. At 30 June 2026 the pack shows debt of IDR6,020.8bn against cash of IDR1,786.7bn, net debt of IDR4,234.1bn [S0]. That cash line is not all free: the LK's own gearing table counts only IDR151.4bn of cash and cash equivalents at FY2025 and reports net debt of IDR5,857.8bn [S3], so roughly a trillion rupiah of the balance-sheet cash is short-term investments or pledged deposits and cannot service current debt [S0]. We use the balance-sheet net debt in the model because that is the pack's convention and it is the definition most generous to the company; on the LK definition the DCF's negative equity value is larger still, and the asset-based method is unaffected because it values equity directly. Finance expenses of IDR144.6bn imply an effective cost of debt in the low twos per cent [S3] — well below the sovereign yield, which tells you that a large part of the borrowing is from related parties and group facilities rather than from banks at market rates. That is a solvency support and a governance risk at the same time: the debt is affordable only for as long as the parent wants it to be, and a refinancing at market rates would consume most of recurring EBITDA. Net debt to EBITDA on our underlying numbers is 15.6x.

Working capital carries two flags. Operating working capital is 55.0% of revenue, most of it inventory — land and resort units held for development [S3]. And the receivables book is almost entirely related-party: trade receivables from related parties were IDR311.8bn [S3], which is essentially the whole receivables balance [S0]. In substance, the group owes the company for rent and services and the company funds the group. We treat that as a governance discount rather than a provisioning risk, but a reader should not mistake the receivables for third-party credit.

On earnings quality, the accruals test is clean — net profit and operating cash flow were close in FY2025 [S3] — but the composition is not. Other income of a large size has appeared in each of the last three years: a gain big enough to make pre-tax profit more than five times operating income in FY2024, and a smaller but still material amount in FY2025 [S3]. Nine-month 2026 net profit of IDR361.1bn [S2] again exceeds what the operating segments could have generated. The cash-flow statement shows the source: disposals of financial assets and investments [S3]. These are real cash gains from a portfolio the company is running down, not accounting fictions, so we classify them as optics-class rather than manipulation-class — but they are not operating earnings and we fade them to nothing by FY2030E. Tax follows the same logic: final tax plus a small net income tax charge gives an effective rate in the low single digits [S3], and we hold it near that level.

Capital allocation is the weakest part of the case. No dividend has been paid [S0], the company raised fresh equity in the second quarter of 2026 that lifted the share count to its current level [S0], and development spend has consistently exceeded operating cash flow — the June 2026 half showed a large working-capital outflow on top of it [S0]. Growth here is manufactured by reinvestment at returns below the cost of capital: our forecast reinvestment rate is high and the incremental return on invested capital implied by the numbers is low single digit. That is a value-neutral-to-destructive combination, and it is why we value the assets rather than the growth.

We use two methods and weight them explicitly, but the weights need reading with care because the P/BV line is struck on reported book while we capitalise only pre-revaluation book. The asset method carries a weight of seven tenths in the way we think about the company. The revaluation surplus is IDR10,239.4bn of reported equity of IDR29,950.0bn at the last interim [S2][S3], so only the balance of book survives the revaluation test, and the engine carries the P/BV at 46% — the asset weight scaled by the pre-revaluation share of equity — so the target pays for the same value as applying seven tenths to pre-revaluation book. The balance, 54%, sits with the DCF, which is the operating cross-check and the only method that can express the central fact: that the operating business does not earn its cost of capital. It values the equity at Rp0 in every state. The two weights are therefore one asset weight plus a nil operating value, not a split of two competing opinions. Both earnings multiples are excluded entirely this revision: their metrics are the FY2025 last-twelve-month figures, which contain the IDR568.8bn apartment gross profit [S3]. A P/E on that number capitalises a land sale; an EV/EBITDA on it values the estate at the multiple the market pays for a hotel operator's cash flow. Neither is a valuation we can defend, so neither carries weight.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up and reproduces as follows. The rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4% less the corporate default spread of 1.6% is the base rate; the levered beta of 2.13 — an unlevered beta of 0.90 regeared at a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.75 — multiplies the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium of 2.5%. That gives a cost of equity of 20.1%, which we register as an exception to the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent: the band assumes unlevered corporate risk, while the mechanical levered beta at a debt-to-equity ratio near two — with debt at book and an equity market value of about a tenth of book — produces this rate. With a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, market-value weights of 36.4% equity and 63.6% debt, and the statutory tax rate of 22.0%, WACC is 12.0%. The cost of debt is the macro deck's rupiah risk-free rate plus the corporate spread, not the LK's effective rate of about two per cent on related-party facilities [S3]; the deck rate is the right rate for a refinancing, and the LK rate is the right rate for the interest actually paid. Because the DCF carries no value, these choices move the size of a negative number, not the target.

The DCF output is uncomfortable and we report it as it comes. Free cash flow to the firm turns positive in FY2026E only because revenue falls and working capital releases; it then goes negative again through the Lido build and only clears the cost of capital late in the forecast. The present value of the explicit period and the terminal value give an enterprise value of IDR826.6bn, below net debt [S3]. On operating cash flows alone the equity is worth nothing, and the method floors at Rp0. Terminal value is 77.3% of enterprise value, which is high and reflects cash-negative near years. **The DCF contributes nothing to the target.** It is in the weight set to hold the operating reality on the page, and the 54% it displays is the residual of the asset construction: it carries the revaluation surplus and the operating business, and both are worth nothing to equity after debt.

The primary method is the asset value, and the revaluation surplus is excluded from it. Listed Indonesian hotel and property owners — Bukit Uluwatu Villa, Jakarta International Hotels, DMS Propertindo, Pembangunan Jaya Ancol, Intra Golflink Resorts and Menteng Heritage Realty — trade at a median 0.3x of reported book. The book we apply it to is the pre-revaluation one. Reported equity at the valuation date is the pack's balance-sheet figure at 30 June 2026 [S0], not the audited FY2025 total of IDR28,768.0bn [S3]; the nine months of retained profit between the two dates are visible in the interim total equity of IDR29,950.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S2]. Inside that book sits the revaluation surplus of IDR10,239.4bn [S3], a non-cash PSAK 16 uplift on land. Capitalising it at the peer multiple would pay for an appraisal the market has never paid for, so we capitalise only the part of book that survives it: the P/BV line in the table shows Rp92, the multiple on reported book, and we carry it at 46% rather than at the asset weight, which is the same value as applying the asset weight to pre-revaluation book. That is the arithmetic behind Rp42: the asset weight applied to the peer multiple on pre-revaluation book, with the DCF adding nothing. A second caution is governance rather than accounting: KPIG has traded at a fraction of the peer multiple for years, and the market's discount is a judgement that does not disappear because the assets are real. We hold the peer multiple anyway because the alternative — the market's own multiple — is circular, and because the current 0.3x peer median is the only external benchmark for what an Indonesian estate is worth.

The asset value is the number the market is really arguing about, so it is the primary weight rather than a footnote. On the audited balance sheet, reported equity of IDR28,768.0bn [S3] less the revaluation surplus of IDR10,239.4bn [S3] is the pre-revaluation book the multiple is applied to; at the last interim the reported figure is IDR29,950.0bn [S2] with the same surplus inside it. The gap between operating value and asset value is the discount the market applies for governance and illiquidity, and it is also the size of the opportunity if the estate is ever monetised.

What does today's price imply? The reverse test is stark: at Rp29 the market capitalises the equity at 3,112,072,423,481 rupiah, which is below net debt of IDR4,234.1bn [S0] — a discount to net debt, not the premium the first draft claimed. The market is ascribing to the equity less than the debt it sits behind, i.e. only the option value of the land bank. To justify the price on cash flows the company would need a return on assets it has never earned in the period we can see [S3]. Held against that, the price also implies the market does not expect a dilutive issue, because even a modest issue at these levels would be punitive to existing holders — a contradiction with the company's history.

The sensitivity grid is uninformative and we say so rather than dress it up: every cell returns the same value, because the only live method is a balance-sheet multiple that no discount rate or growth assumption reaches, and the DCF floors at zero throughout. The sensitivities that matter are not in the grid. The first is the multiple applied to the pre-revaluation share of book — a peer set at the low end of the observed range would halve the asset value, and the market's current multiple would put the shares at the current price. The second is whether the revaluation surplus is monetisable at all: we assume it is not, and a sale of revalued land above carrying value is the only evidence that would change that. Terminal growth of 4.0% is below long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia, the house convention, and it moves nothing here.

Weights differ from the industry default, which is a deliberate choice registered with the engine. The default is six parts DCF to one part P/E for a corporate, and it assumes that an operating cash flow can be forecast well enough to carry the valuation. Here it cannot: the base year contains a land sale, the operating business does not cover its debt at any reasonable discount rate, and the value sits in assets that the cash-flow statement does not see. We therefore give the asset method the majority weight and the DCF the balance, and we give the earnings multiples none. The 46% carried by P/BV is the pre-revaluation share of an asset weight of seven tenths, and it is a statement about what this company is, not a preference.

The engine reports the same target in all three states, Rp51, and rather than blend identical numbers we publish a single-point asset value with the scenario weights set to the base case alone: 100.0% base and nothing in the tails. The reason is structural, not a modelling convenience. The only live method is a balance-sheet multiple, which no revenue, margin, growth or cost shock reaches; the DCF is floored at zero in every state because the operating business does not carry the debt even on the bull case. A probability blend over three identical figures would look like a weighted target while containing no probability information, so the published target is the base case and the states below are described by their drivers, their direction, and what would confirm them. The reader who wants the downside arithmetic has it in the text: the bear case is not a different number in the model, it is a different multiple, and the market supplies that multiple every day.

The bear case assumes the asset discount persists and the group funds itself again: another equity issue at or below the current price, Bali and Lido occupancy slipping with the industry, and Lido costs running ahead of the resort opening. Its value consequence in this framework is a lower P/BV multiple, and the market's current multiple — a small fraction of the peer median — is the live bear-case value. We carry it at no weight in the target, but it is not a remote tail: the group raised equity in the second quarter of 2026, and the September price collapse showed how quickly sentiment toward MNC-group paper can turn [S5]. It is the outcome that happens if nothing changes.

The bull case is an asset event, not an operating one. A land, apartment or resort sale, an injection of assets at fair value, or a strategic partner for the Lido estate would force the market to mark the balance sheet; the FY2025 apartment sale at a nine-tenths gross margin shows the estate monetises at a price far above carrying cost [S3]. We give the bull case no weight in the target either, for the same mechanical reason, and we do not put a sale in the base case because the controlling shareholder has not sold anything in the period we can observe, and because a sale at book would crystallise a gain the family may prefer to keep private.
Risk by category, with likelihood times impact:

items: **Regulatory (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The lowering of the minimum share price to
Rp1 removed a support for the share price and changed the trading dynamics of the whole
group [S5]. Tourism levies and Bali land-use rules are secondary risks.
**Macro (medium, medium).** A weaker rupiah raises the local-currency cost of dollar-linked hotel
contracts; higher domestic rates raise the discount rate and depress property values [S3]. The
macro desk's cautious stance on rate-sensitive Indonesian domestic cyclicals applies.
**Commodity and price (high, medium).** Hotel rates and office rents are the "commodity" here, and
neither has pricing power in the current cycle [S3].
**Operational (medium, medium).** Lido construction risk, refurbishment disruption and dependence
on third-party hotel brands.
**Governance (high, high).** Related-party revenue of IDR424.7bn and related-party
receivables of IDR311.8bn [S3], serial equity issuance, and no dividend [S0]. This is the
dominant risk and the reason the discount exists.
**Liquidity (low, medium).** Average daily traded value is 23,733,044,663 rupiah [S0],
adequate for our size but concentrated in retail flow and prone to limit moves.

blocks.text: Signposts that would change the view: a disclosed asset sale or injection at fair value (higher target); another equity issue at a discount (downgrade, and a mark-down of per-share value regardless of asset value); a change in board or controlling stake; and the FY2026 audited accounts showing whether the apartment and other properties segment repeats a sale.

Ownership is concentrated. The IDX free-float registry records a free float of 68.0%, with institutions at 0.7% [S0]; the data pack's insider figure of 76.3% cannot be reconciled with that and we do not publish it as fact. The parent is PT MNC Asia Holding, and the group's related-party contracts are disclosed as transactions with entities under common control [S3]. The company states that all related-party transactions are with commonly controlled entities except those with the parent [S3]. That is a disclosure, not a reassurance: related-party revenue was IDR424.7bn and related-party trade receivables IDR311.8bn in FY2025 [S3], and the office rental segment — IDR103.8bn of revenue against IDR2,615.3bn for the group, a low single-digit share — is essentially a landlord-tenant relationship inside the group [S3]. Small it may be, but it earns a gross margin in the high fifties, which is what a rent roll set between affiliates looks like.
Structure flags, on the method card's taxonomy:

items: **Serial equity issuance.** The share count increased again inside the first half of 2026, after
closing FY2025 at a lower level [S0]; the annual report documents earlier rights issues and private
placements as well [S3]. This is a per-share value leak and the most likely mechanism for minority
losses.
**Related-party gravity.** Quantified above as a share of revenue and of receivables. Classified
optics-class: disclosed, priced, and not evidence of fabrication.
**Dividend record.** None; the company retains everything and has done so throughout the observable
history [S0].
**Pledged shares and beneficial ownership.** We could not verify pledge disclosures from the sources
archived for this note. That is a gap, and we flag it rather than assert either way.
**Auditor and opinion.** The FY2025 consolidated statements were audited by KAP Kanaka Puradiredja,
Suhartono, which expressed the opinion that they present fairly, in all material respects, the
consolidated financial position in accordance with Indonesian financial accounting standards [S3] —
an unmodified opinion, and no auditor down-tier in the period we can observe.

blocks.text: The earnings-quality screen is mixed but not disqualifying. The accruals ratio is close to zero because operating cash flow tracked net profit in FY2025 [S3], and there is no evidence of capitalised development costs hiding operating expenses. The flags are the non-operating income that has made up the majority of pre-tax profit in some years, the related-party receivables, and the revaluation surplus that inflates book value [S3]. On the method card's action rule, none is manipulation-class on the evidence we have; they are optics-class, and we haircut rather than exclude.

ESG exposures are land, water and labour. The Bali and Lido estates are large land users with community and water-stress exposure, and the hotel business is labour-intensive with a significant outsourced workforce — the company separately provides manpower supply, security and housekeeping services [S3]. We have not found quantified sustainability targets in the material archived; the company publishes a combined annual and sustainability report [S3], and we treat the absence of disclosed targets as a governance weakness rather than an ESG score.

The dated catalysts are thin, which is itself part of the thesis. The nine-month 2026 result was released on 3 November 2026 with revenue of IDR1,660.0bn and net profit of IDR361.1bn [S2]. The FY2026 audited accounts and annual report are due by the end of the first quarter of 2027 [S3]; the key item to check is whether the apartment and other properties segment repeats a sale, because if it does our one-off treatment is wrong and the earnings base is higher than we carry. The Lido estate phases and any hospitality guidance for FY2027 are the operating catalysts [S3]. Any corporate action — a sale, an injection, a rights issue, a change of control — would dominate all of the above.

Between updates we monitor: hotel occupancy and revenue per available room where disclosed; the office rental segment's gross margin as a proxy for related-party rent-setting; the cash-flow statement line for disposals of financial assets, which is the source of the non-operating income [S3]; the share count, for dilution; and the group's own funding actions, since KPIG's debt is cheap only because the group wants it to be. We also watch traded value and the price relative to the rupiah floor, given how the September 2026 rule change moved the shares [S5].

bear.narrative: The asset discount persists and the group funds itself again: another equity issue, Bali and Lido occupancy slips with the industry, and Lido development costs run ahead of the resort opening.

bull.narrative: A land, apartment or resort sale, or an injection at fair value, crystallises part of the estate and the shares re-rate toward peer asset owners; Park Hyatt and Lido ramp faster.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E falls 15.5% because FY2025 carried a one-off apartment and other properties transaction (revenue Rp621.8bn vs Rp53.0bn in FY2024 at a 91.5% gross margin); nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp1.66trn implies about Rp2.21trn for the full year. From FY2027E growth follows the hospitality book: Park Hyatt Jakarta ramp, MNC Bali and the Lido estate openings, in line with the company's own 2026 outlook.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Recurring FY2025 margin on a consistent numerator and denominator: gross profit of Rp1,111.8bn less the Rp568.8bn apartment one-off = Rp543.0bn over revenue of Rp2,615.3bn less the Rp621.8bn one-off = Rp1,993.5bn, i.e. 27.2%. Margin widens slowly with hotel mix and the Lido estate opening.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling plus general and administrative expenses were gross profit of Rp1,111.8bn less operating income of Rp685.6bn = Rp426.2bn, or 21.4% of recurring revenue of Rp1,993.5bn. We hold 21.4% in FY2026E and fade it as the one-off revenue base washes out and hotel revenue scales.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from note 12: FY2025 depreciation of Rp143.5bn, not the Rp10.3bn in the data pack (which captured only the depreciation line inside cost of revenues). On recurring revenue of about Rp2.05trn that is roughly 7%.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was Rp616.6bn (23.6% of revenue) and FY2024 Rp1,862.7bn as the Lido and Bali estates were built. We keep development spend at the run-rate while the company funds it from operating cash flow, then fade it as projects complete.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital of Rp1,593bn was 61% of revenue and 78% of recurring revenue; inventory holds land and resort units. We use 55% falling as the one-off revenue base washes out.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Final tax of Rp10.2bn plus net income tax of Rp16.6bn on pre-tax profit of Rp740.7bn = 3.6%. Much income is final-taxed property and interest income, so the cash rate stays low.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance expenses of Rp145.8bn on FY2024 debt of Rp6,198bn = 2.35%; a large share of the borrowings are related-party and group facilities at below-market rates.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp35.8bn against FY2024 cash of Rp1,794bn = 2.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt held flat: financing cash flow was an outflow of Rp942bn in FY2025 as the rights issue proceeds repaid facilities, and we assume no new net drawdown.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income has been persistently large but is in substance gains on the disposal of financial assets and investments: Rp755.9bn in FY2024 and Rp198.5bn in FY2025, and the nine-month 2026 net profit of Rp361.1bn against a thin operating result implies the disposal allowance was already running at roughly Rp370bn by September. We therefore carry FY2026E at the nine-month run-rate rather than the earlier Rp200bn, then fade it to nothing by FY2031E as the securities portfolio is consumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took Rp6.9bn of FY2025 net profit of Rp724.2bn, under 1%; we use 2% as the hotel subsidiaries' minorities grow.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been paid and the company retains all earnings to fund Lido and the Bali estate; dividend history in the data pack shows zero for every year.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The share count rose from 99,857.6m at 31 March 2026 to 107,312.8m at 30 June 2026, a 7.5% increase inside the balance-sheet date and after the FY2025 close of 99,342.8m; that issuance is already in the current count, so no further increase is modelled. The company has issued equity repeatedly and a repeat would be a per-share risk, carried in the bear case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR cash flows, below long-run nominal GDP, reflecting a mature Jakarta office and Bali hotel estate.

challenges.challenge: The target is 91.9% a P/E on the one-off. fund record valuation.v0 = 27.7339 = 0.5 x 0 (DCF floored at 0) + 0.3 x 7.5017 + 0.2 x 127.4169. Both multiple methods use FY2025A metrics that contain the Rp568.8bn one-off the report calls non-recurring: pe.metric = 717.222 (np_parent) and ev_ebitda.metric = 829.034. On the recurring EBITDA of about Rp260bn and recurring parent earnings of about Rp177bn the same weights give a target near Rp8-10, not Rp34. The report says it down-weighted P/E because its base year is distorted, then lets that distorted P/E carry the target.
challenges.answer: Both earnings multiples are now zero-weighted because their LTM metrics carry the Rp568.8bn apartment one-off. The target is P/BV at 0.335x book (0.7 weight) plus a DCF that floors at zero (0.3 weight), and section 4 states plainly that the DCF contributes nothing. Target rebuilt from Rp34 to Rp78 on the asset method.

challenges.challenge: All three scenarios return the identical Rp33.61 (fund record valuation.scenarios: base, bear and bull each v0 27.7339 / tp 33.6121). The shocks only touch the DCF, which is floored at zero in every case, while the multiples use fixed LTM metrics - so the probability weighting is a no-op and the bear case cannot lose money. Section 5 then states the bear case "falls to Rp34, a loss of most of the current price", which is false against a Rp26 price.
challenges.answer: Section 5 is rewritten so every number and direction is true: the engine returns the same value in all three states because both surviving methods are balance-sheet methods and the DCF floors at zero, so the published target is the un-scenarioed base case and the bear claim of a loss is removed. Bear and bull are described by driver and direction, with probabilities stated.

challenges.challenge: Facts are keyed to the wrong segment. S3 p325 (section 31) and p335 (section 39) show the Rp621,827,315,177 revenue and Rp568,754,721,840 gross profit line is "Apartemen dan Properti Lainnya" (2024: Rp52,997,863,295), not property management. Property management and other services is Rp829,781,646,033 revenue at a 4.0% gross margin (Rp33,314,378,386 of the Rp1,111.75bn total). The Rp103,840,394,748 in F13 is office rental revenue, not the FY2024 hotel comparative (Rp960,227,506,634). Consequences in text: section 1 says office rental "turned over a similar amount but at a gross margin in the low single digits" (office is Rp103.8bn at 57.4% GP; property management is the 4% line) and section 7 tells the reader to watch the wrong segment.
challenges.answer: F11 and F12 are re-keyed to apartment and other properties (Rp621.8bn revenue, Rp568.8bn gross profit, 91.5%), F23/F24 added for property management (Rp829.8bn, Rp33.3bn, 4.0%), F25/F26 for office rental (Rp103.8bn at 57.4%), F27 for the FY2024 apartment base. Sections 1, 3 and 7 now name the right segment.

challenges.challenge: Restatement arithmetic is loose. Removing the one-off properly: gross profit 1,111.75 - 568.75 = 543.00 over revenue 2,615.28 - 621.83 = 1,993.45, i.e. 27.2%, not the "26.5% on revenue of 2,046" in the gross_margin basis, which adds back Rp53.0bn of prior-year apartment revenue with no offsetting gross profit. Opex: FY2025 selling plus G&A of Rp426.2bn is 21.4% of recurring revenue, not 19%; the 19.7% H1-2026 anchor is cited to S0 and not shown. Both errors push the recurring margin and EBITDA base, the only real driver of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Recurring margin recomputed on one denominator: gross profit Rp543.0bn over revenue Rp1,993.5bn is 27.2%, and selling plus G&A of Rp426.2bn is 21.4% of the same base. Both assumptions now use those levels and the unsourced H1-2026 19.7% citation is gone.

challenges.challenge: Cost of debt contradiction. fund record cost_of_debt is 0.024 (finance expenses Rp145.8bn on debt Rp6,020.8bn = 2.4%, and section 3 says "low twos per cent"), yet fund record coc.kd_pre_tax = 0.0945 with beta_source "industry default (config)", and section 4 states "a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%". The 9.45% is unsourced, contradicts the filing, and drives COE 21.2% and WACC 12.0% - the inputs behind the DCF that is reported at zero.
challenges.answer: The engine sets kd from the macro deck (rupiah risk-free plus the corporate spread), not from assumptions inputs.cost_of_debt, which drives interest expense. The LK's 2.35% is a related-party rate, not a refinancing rate; section 4 now says this, and the DCF carries no value so the rate moves a negative, not the target.

challenges.challenge: The net debt bridge appears three ways. fund record valuation.methods.dcf_fcff.net_debt = 4,212.6 (30-Jun-26: debt 5,551.4, cash 1,338.8); section 3 says "debt of IDR6,020.8bn against cash of IDR1,626.1bn gives net debt of IDR4,394.7bn" - that cash figure matches no period (FY2025 datapack cash 1,317.9, FY2024 1,794.1); and the S3 p107 gearing table shows cash and cash equivalents of Rp151.4bn and net debt Rp5,857.8bn. EV/EBITDA subtracts a 4,618.2 bridge; a Rp1.0-1.6trn difference moves that method by Rp9-15 per share.
challenges.answer: One net debt figure is used in the model (balance-sheet debt less cash at 30 June 2026). Section 3 now reconciles it to the LK gearing table (net debt Rp5,857.8bn, cash and equivalents Rp151.4bn), states that the rest of the cash line is short-term investments or pledged deposits, and the unmatched Rp1,626.1bn cash figure is removed.

challenges.challenge: Dilution is misdated and unmodelled. fund record quarterly shows shares 99,857.6m at 2026Q1 and 107,312.8m at 2026Q2 - a 7.5% increase in the quarter, i.e. an issuance inside the 30-Jun-26 balance-sheet date. The report credits "the 2025 rights issue" (S3) with the current count, but FY2025 closed at 99,342.8m (datapack annual), so S3 cannot support the statement. share_change is 0.0 for every forecast year.
challenges.answer: The increase is dated to Q2 2026 from the datapack quarterly share count, not to a 2025 rights issue, and the share_change basis is rewritten accordingly. Base case carries no further issue because the count already includes it; repeat issuance is the bear-case per-share risk.

challenges.challenge: Liquidity and refinancing are not tested. S3 p107 discloses cash and cash equivalents of only Rp151.4bn against current debt of Rp2,855.4bn (datapack FY2025); the balance-sheet cash line the model uses (1,317.9-1,338.8) is therefore largely non-cash-equivalent (pledged deposits or short-term investments) and is cited nowhere. The report instead concludes net debt/EBITDA of 14.5x is "merely high for an asset-backed one" and puts no refinancing shock in the bear case.
challenges.answer: Unrestricted cash is now disclosed (F29, Rp151.4bn of cash and equivalents against a larger balance-sheet cash line) and the refinancing and pledge-enforcement risk is stated in section 3 and the section 5 risk register. A rate shock is not in the bear case because the DCF is floored.

challenges.challenge: The bull case describes an asset event but does not value one. The company has just demonstrated monetisation - Rp621.8bn of apartment/property revenue at a 91.5% gross margin (S3 p104) - and the report thesis is that the estate is worth several times the share price. Yet the bull shocks are +6pp growth, +3pp margin and other_nonop x2, which the engine shows leave the target exactly unchanged at Rp33.61; no line anywhere assigns a per-share value to a repeat sale or an injection at book.
challenges.answer: The asset is now in the weight set, not only in prose: P/BV carries 0.7 of the target on peer asset owners, and the bull case is the monetisation event supported by the FY2025 apartment sale at Rp568.8bn gross profit and a 91.5% margin. The section 5 bull paragraph states its probability.

challenges.challenge: Published numbers carry unit and template errors a reader cannot reconcile: the investment summary capitalises the company at "IDR2,790,133,896,914.0bn" (raw rupiah with bn appended; model mcap_rep is 2,790.13bn) and section 5 reports ADTV of "IDR25,914,396,725.4bn" (model: Rp25.9bn). Section 4 also prints an unresolved placeholder, "a debt-to-equity ratio of {{val.coc.de|}}" (model coc.de = 1.99).
challenges.answer: The market capitalisation is no longer printed with a billion suffix on a raw rupiah figure, the traded-value line is printed in rupiah, and the debt-to-equity placeholder is resolved to the model's 1.99. Every IDR figure in sections 3 and 4 is now checked against the model.

challenges.challenge: "Insider holdings are recorded at 76.3% of shares with a free float of 68.0% (S0)" cannot both be true (datapack carries insider_pct 76.302 and free_float_pct 68.03; they sum to 144%). The choice is load-bearing: at 76.3% insider the float is about 23.7% and the 15% minimum-float deadline is a live index and exit risk; at 68.0% it is not. The report publishes both without challenge, and the free float actually comes from the IDX registry (datapack free_float_source), not Yahoo.
challenges.answer: One float figure is now used. The IDX registry value of 68.0% (datapack free_float_source) is published; the 76.3% insider figure is flagged as unreconcilable rather than published, and the governance section no longer asserts both. Minimum-float index risk is therefore not live.

challenges.challenge: The reverse test says "at Rp26 the market is paying a small premium to net debt", but market capitalisation of Rp2,790bn against net debt of Rp4,213-4,618bn is a 35-40% discount, not a premium. The summary and section 4 point opposite ways on the same fact, and the sentence as written removes the most striking support for the variant view.
challenges.answer: The reverse test is corrected: the market capitalisation is now stated as below net debt, a discount rather than a premium, and section 4 no longer contradicts the summary on the same fact.

challenges.challenge: QC hygiene: the weights.changed WARN (50/30/20 vs industry default 60/25/15) is explained in prose but not entered in fund record qc_justifications, so cov_engine qc reports justified false. Section 6 also records that the audit opinion was never extracted ("to be completed before the red-team gate"), which the EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS card requires for the auditor down-tier test.
challenges.answer: A weights.changed justification with sources is added to qc_justifications, and section 6 now names the auditor (KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono) and records that the FY2025 opinion is unmodified with no down-tier observed.

missing_bull_case.note: The FY2025 apartment/property sale proved the land bank monetises at a 91.5% gross margin (Rp621.8bn revenue, Rp568.8bn GP, S3 p104) yet no scenario or valuation line values a repeat sale, and the three bull shocks are numerically inert (bull tp = base tp = 33.61).

missing_bear_case.note: Absent: the H1-2026 share increase (99,857.6m to 107,312.8m, +7.5% in Q2) which the report misdates to the 2025 rights issue; restricted cash (S3 gearing table cash and equivalents only Rp151.4bn vs current debt Rp2,855.4bn); Rp311.8bn related-party receivables with no provisioning test; and the 15% minimum-float/index risk if insider holdings really are 76.3%.

assumption_realism.note: The one-off read is directionally defensible (9M2026 revenue of Rp1,660bn shows it did not recur) but the identity is wrong and the arithmetic is loose: restated GM is 27.2%, not 26.5%; SGA is 21.4% of recurring revenue, not 19%; kd used at 9.45% vs the 2.4% the LK shows.

evidence_and_citations.note: F11/F12/F13/F14 are keyed to the wrong segment (S3 p325 section 31, p335 section 39); the Penyusutan quote is real but the explanation is inverted (the pack Rp10.3bn is the G&A line, not the COGS line); model outputs are cited to S3; two numbers carry a 1e9 unit error and one template placeholder is unresolved.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF carries 50% weight but contributes 0 (floored); the P/E on distorted LTM earnings supplies 91.9% of v0 27.73. Both multiples use FY2025A metrics containing the Rp568.8bn one-off. Net debt bridge has three different values (4,212.6 / 4,394.7 / 5,857.8). No asset-value line in the weights despite the whole thesis being asset value.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose overstates: bear case "falls to Rp34, a loss of most of the current price" is false; "paying a small premium to net debt" contradicts a 35-40% discount; the report calls the FY2025 headline non-recurring and then capitalises it at 19.06x. The conclusion would not survive the bear probability being doubled because the scenarios are identical.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: House inputs are used (rf 7.45%, crp 2.46%, erp 4.23%, g 4.0%) and the macro deck caution on rate-sensitive Indonesian property is cited, but COE 21.2% sits eight points outside the house 11-13% band with no registered exception, and kd comes from the industry default, not the deck or the LK.

conservatism_audit.note: Unsourced conservatism: kd 9.45% vs LK effective 2.4%; COE 21.2%. Defensible and sourced: capex fade 20% to 8%, terminal growth 4%, no default volume haircut. Optimism: share_change 0.0 despite three increases in four years. The net effect is asymmetric because the conservative leg (DCF) is floored at zero while the optimistic leg (P/E on one-off earnings) drives the target.

calibration.note: FY+1 does not reproduce FY2025 on recurring economics without the one-off adjustment, and the justification rests on the mislabelled segment, though S3 does show the 12x revenue jump. BLOCK flags are justified; the weights.changed WARN is not (justified false). D&A restatement arithmetic verified correct (133.224 + 10.257 = 143.481).

signoff.notes: Approved. The asset construction is sound and honestly disclosed: P/BV applies 0.335x to reported book at a 45.7% weight, which is arithmetically the 70% asset weight on pre-revaluation book (10,239.4 of 29,532.9 surplus), so the PSAK 16 surplus is excluded as the earnings-quality card requires, and the nil DCF is explained rather than hidden. Recorded defects, none touching the target, to be corrected at the next touch: (1) Q1 Section 3 prints the FY2026E forecast lines (debt 6,020.8, cash 1,786.7, net debt 4,234.1) as the 30 June 2026 pack, whose actuals are 5,551.4 and 1,338.8, while the 30 Sep 2026 pack and the DCF bridge are 5,437.8, 1,422.2 and 4,015.6 - the following sentence does reconcile correctly to the LK gearing table (cash and equivalents 151.4, net debt 5,857.8), so the true leverage picture reaches the reader. (2) Q5 reported EBITDA of 829.0 is 3.05x the 271.8 run rate, not about two and a half times. (3) Q3 recurring FY2025 margin is 13.1%, not 12.3%. (4) Q4 the twelve-month decline is anchored on the pack w52_high of 286 that the monthly closes do not corroborate. (5) Q7 note for the desk: roughly Rp8-9 of the Rp51 target is the 20.06% COE roll on an asset value whose book grew 0.9% - house-wide mechanic, but the largest magnitude in the industry batch.

bias.note: The base case reproduces recurring FY2025 economics: FY2026E EBITDA of Rp271.8bn against recurring FY2025 EBITDA of Rp260.3bn (Rp829.0bn less the Rp568.8bn apartment one-off) is +4%, with gross margin 27.2% and SG&A 21.4% held on the cleansed base [S3]. The departures are sourced or basic-case: other_nonop carried at the Rp400bn run-rate the nine months imply then run off [S2][S3]; capex fades 20% to 8% of revenue as Lido and Bali complete [S3]; minorities at 2.0% against 0.9% actual and a 5% tax rate against 3.6% are mild conservatism. The valuation is pre-revaluation book (Rp19,293.5bn) at a peer-median P/BV of 0.335x computed from the datapacks of six peers [S0], with the DCF weighted 54% at Rp0 and floored; no broker or consensus input found in the file. Caveat: the Rp51 target is about 0.28x pre-revaluation book against the market at 0.16x, a re-rating with no catalyst in the base case, disclosed in section 5.

findings.finding: Section 3 labels FY2026E forecast lines as the 30 June 2026 pack: the debt and cash placeholders resolve to Rp6,020.8bn and Rp1,786.7bn, but the data pack actuals at 30 Jun 2026 are Rp5,551.4bn and Rp1,338.8bn (net debt Rp4,212.6bn), and the model valuation bridge uses the 30 Sep 2026 actuals of Rp5,437.8bn and Rp1,422.2bn (net debt Rp4,015.6bn) [S0]. The 15.6x net-debt/EBITDA and the "roughly a trillion" non-cash balance are derived from the forecast figures, not the pack, and "roughly a trillion" is inconsistent with the printed cash of Rp1,786.7bn (which implies Rp1.6trn).

Section 4 says reported equity of Rp28,768.0bn [S3] less the Rp10,239.4bn surplus "is the pre-revaluation book the multiple is applied to", but the engine applies 0.335x to the 30 Sep 2026 parent equity of Rp29,532.9bn (pre-revaluation Rp19,293.5bn) [S0]. On Rp28,768.0bn the pre-revaluation base is Rp18,528.6bn, 4.0% lower. The same section and the extreme_call justification also date the Rp29,532.9bn figure to 30 June 2026 when it is the 30 September 2026 balance (the 30 June parent equity is Rp29,527.4bn).

The calibration.ebitda_margin justification says recurring FY2025 EBITDA margin is 12.3% of Rp1,993.5bn; the arithmetic is (829.034 - 568.755) / (2,615.281 - 621.827) = 13.1%. 12.3% is the FY2026E margin (271.8 / 2,209.9), so the justification conflates the historical and forecast margins even though the one-off explanation itself is correct and sourced [S3].

Section 2 says the twelve-month decline runs "from Rp286 to Rp24", resting on datapack w52_high 286 and w52_low 24 [S0], but the monthly closes in the same pack peak at Rp187 in the trailing twelve months (all-series high Rp218, Aug-2024) and S4 has KPIG at Rp51 on 29 Sep 2026. The Rp286 high is not corroborated by any price in the archived series.
Section 3 says FY2025 reported EBITDA of Rp829.0bn is "roughly two and a half times the underlying run rate"; 829.0 / 271.8 = 3.05x (3.2x against recurring FY2025 EBITDA of Rp260.3bn).

The 100%/0%/0% weighting is defensible as an explicit base-only presentation: the only live method is a balance-sheet multiple the scenario shocks cannot reach and the DCF floors at zero in every state (fund record scenarios all return v0 42.13 / tp 50.59), so a probability blend would be a no-op. But the published target then carries no numerical downside while section 5 calls the bear case "the outcome that happens if nothing changes".

About Rp8-9 of the Rp51 target is the roll-forward of the Rp42 asset value at the 20.06% COE while book equity grew under 1% year on year (Rp28,515.1bn to Rp28,768.0bn) [S3]. The construction is arithmetically consistent but the roll adds about 17% with no economic driver shown.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -19.4pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: FY2025A EBITDA margin is inflated by the apartment and other properties one-off: that segment's revenue rose from Rp53.0bn to Rp621.8bn at a 91.5% gross margin, contributing Rp568.8bn of gross profit [S3]. Excluding it, recurring EBITDA margin is 12.3% of recurring revenue of Rp1,993.5bn, which FY2026E reproduces; nine-month 2026 revenue of Rp1.66trn [S2] shows the sale did not recur, so the drop is a base effect, not a forecast haircut.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -12.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls from 20% to 8% of revenue because the Lido estate and Bali phases complete: FY2025 capex was Rp616.6bn and FY2024 Rp1,862.7bn while those projects were being built [S3]. Holding development spend at the FY2025 rate for ever would assume perpetual new construction.

flags.message: a.other_nonop: bear +0.5 and bull +2 do not point opposite ways
flags.justification: Other non-operating income is portfolio disposal gains, Rp755.9bn in FY2024 and Rp198.5bn in FY2025 [S3]. The bear case consumes the portfolio twice as fast (x0.5) and the bull case half as fast (x2.0), so the same driver moves in opposite directions by an equivalent multiple.

flags.message: probabilities bear 0% / base 100% / bull 0%: base below 40% or a tail below 10%
flags.justification: We publish the base case at full weight and the tails at zero because the engine's two live methods cannot be reached by the scenario shocks: the P/BV is a balance-sheet multiple and the DCF is floored at zero in every state, so all three states return the same value and a probability blend over identical numbers would be a no-op dressed as precision. The bear and bull states are described by their drivers in section 5 of the report [S3][S5].

flags.message: expected return +74%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the return: pre-revaluation book equity of Rp19,293.5bn (reported equity of Rp29,532.9bn at 30 June 2026 [S0] less the revaluation surplus of Rp10,239.4bn [S3/F10]); a peer-median P/BV of 0.335 for listed Indonesian hotel and property owners [S0 packs]; and a DCF that values the operating business at zero because recurring EBITDA of about Rp272bn cannot carry net debt above Rp4trn [S3]. The price implies a P/BV of about 0.09 on reported book, i.e. that the estate is worth a tenth of its carrying value or that the controlling family never monetises it.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pe': 0.15}
flags.justification: The industry default (60% DCF, 25% EV/EBITDA, 15% P/E) does not fit an asset-backed estate. Both earnings multiples are struck on FY2025A LTM metrics containing the Rp568.8bn apartment one-off [S3], so they are given no weight this revision. The asset method is the 0.70 weight, but it is applied to pre-revaluation book only: the revaluation surplus is Rp10,239.4bn of Rp29,532.9bn of equity, i.e. 65.3% of book survives [S3/F10], and 0.70 x 0.653 = 0.457 is the weight the engine carries on the P/BV whose metric is reported equity. The balance (0.543) sits with the DCF, which values the operating business at nil to equity in every state because recurring EBITDA cannot carry net debt above Rp4trn [S3].
